question: Does test-driven development actually reduce defect rates in production software, and what does it cost in development time? Weigh the empirical evidence — controlled experiments, industrial case studies, and meta-analyses — rather than practitioner opinion. Where studies disagree, explain what accounts for the disagreement. Give the strongest honest case both for and against adopting it.
summary: The retrieved empirical record does not answer the question as posed: every study whose citation survived audit measures a proxy — percentage of experimenter-written oracle tests passed on toy tasks (arXiv:2011.11942), or functional correctness on a single assigned development task (arXiv:1611.05994) — not production or post-release defects. Where the comparison is controlled and pooled, TDD does not win: across a family of 12 experiments the random-effects estimate favours iterative test-last (ITL) by 7.06 percentage points (95% CI -14.47 to 0.35, non-significant, I-squared 67.8%). When the process is dissected, test-first ordering ("sequencing") had "no important influence" on quality or productivity; improvements tracked granularity and uniformity, leading those authors to conclude the claimed benefits "may not be due to its distinctive test-first dynamic" but to the fine-grained, steady steps TDD-like processes encourage. On cost, the strongest surviving industrial source reports only a "moderate perceived" productivity loss with no measured effort effect size and no dispersion, and a 2020 review of a decade of top-venue TDD research found no study at all on managing the test suite TDD generates, with one eight-year industrial report finding test code grows faster than production code. The industrial studies that motivate adoption are non-randomized with size-mismatched comparators (MSN: 26.0 source KLOC / 46 man-months / 5-8 developers versus 149.0 KLOC / 144 man-months / 12 developers) and, at the Microsoft sites, no enforcement or monitoring that test-first was actually followed. The strongest honest case FOR adoption in this corpus is mechanistic and observational — one IBM team sustained TDD across five years and ten-plus releases, and TDD induces exactly the small, uniform steps that did correlate with quality and productivity — while the case AGAINST is that the test-first ordering itself has no demonstrated effect over an equally iterative alternative, and its lifecycle cost has never been measured.

findings.claim: The premise of the question is not testable against this evidence base: the surviving studies measure lab/controlled-setting proxies for quality, not production or post-release defect rates.
findings.evidence: The 12-experiment family defines its sole response variable as "the percentage of successful tests in the test battery—or test oracle—that we (i.e., the experimenters) built to test participant solutions" (QLTY = #Tests(Pass)/#Tests(All)*100%), on five toy tasks (MarsRover, Bowling Scorekeeper, MusicPhone, Sudoku, Spread-Sheet), with participants having "no access to these test oracles"; the paper's own threats section states "our findings are limited exclusively to toy tasks... may not be representative of what may happen when developing real-life industrial systems," and the word "defect" appears nowhere in it. Fucci et al.'s dissection states "Quality was measured by functional correctness" over "82 data points collected from 39 professionals, each capturing the process used while performing a specific development task." Coverage analysis of the whole corpus found NOT ONE source measuring clean post-release or customer-reported field defects, so the proxy-versus-field comparison the question invites cannot be run — the field-defect arm is empty, not merely small.
findings.citationCheck: supported (all three sources; the operationalization details for arXiv:2011.11942 and arXiv:2007.09863 sit in the full text behind the abstract landing page, not in the abstract itself)
findings.vote: 2-1 on the proxy-measure and review claims; 3-0 on the Fucci outcome-measure claim

findings.claim: Pooled across 12 controlled experiments, TDD did not beat iterative test-last; the point estimate runs the other way and is not significant.
findings.evidence: Random-effects meta-analysis of all 12 experiments (academia and industry): "ITL achieves higher quality than TDD (M=-7.06, 95% CI=(-14.47, 0.35)). However, this difference in performance is not statistically significant (as the 95% CI crosses 0), and small... Additionally, there is a medium heterogeneity of results (I^2=67.8%, Q-statistic=39.70, p-value=<<0.001)." Units are percentage points of oracle-test pass rate. Scope conditions the paper itself attaches and that must travel with this number: TDD novices, toy tasks, and "the results vary largely across the individual experiments." This is a null-to-reversed result against an equally iterative control, not against no testing.

findings.claim: Test-first ordering is not the active ingredient. When the TDD process is decomposed, sequencing shows no important influence; the association with quality and productivity sits with small, uniform steps — which are a confound of TDD rather than TDD's defining feature.
findings.evidence: Abstract, Result: "Quality and productivity improvements were primarily positively associated with the granularity and uniformity. Sequencing, the order in which test and production code are written, had no important influence." Abstract, Conclusion: "The claimed benefits of TDD may not be due to its distinctive test-first dynamic, but rather due to the fact that TDD-like processes encourage fine-grained, steady steps that improve focus and flow." The analysis is regression over 82 data points from 39 professionals, so the relations are associational (the paper says "associated with"), not experimentally isolated; the paper's fourth characteristic, refactoring effort, was negatively associated with both outcomes. This is the single most decision-relevant surviving finding: it says that if TDD helps, the thing to adopt may be step size, not test-first ordering.
findings.vote: 2-1 on both the sequencing/granularity claim and the conclusion claim

findings.claim: The cost side of the surviving industrial evidence is an argument, not a measurement: the productivity cost is reported as 'perceived' and 'moderate', with no effect size and no dispersion, and is asserted to be compensated by quality gains.
findings.evidence: The paper's own wording: "This quality improvement would compensate for the moderate perceived productivity losses." Full-text retrieval confirms no effort measurement exists in the paper: "The team did not keep time records. However, on the survey we asked the developers for their perception of how much overall time it took to write the unit tests" — a spread of ten developers' self-reported perceptions (one no extra time, one <5%, two 5-10%, one 11-20%, two 21-25%, three >25%). The compensation argument imports an external break-even rule from another study rather than measuring lifecycle cost. Note the trap avoided: this paper contains a table of 25-35% / 15% development-time increases, but that table summarises other authors' Microsoft case studies, not this IBM team's measured cost.
findings.citationCheck: supported (verified at abstract level on the paywalled publisher page; the absence of a measured effort effect size was additionally confirmed against a recovered full text)

findings.claim: Lifecycle cost — maintaining the test suite TDD generates — is essentially unstudied, and the one long-horizon industrial data point runs the wrong way: test code grew faster than production code.
findings.evidence: A 2020 review of TDD research "published in top venues in the past decade": "understanding effects such as the actual maintenance costs that manifest themselves only when the software is in use has not received enough attention in research. Especially, test suites could grow faster than production code in TDD [43], but we have not seen any study that concern managing tests." Reference [43] is Sundelin, Gonzalez-Huerta & Wnuk (2018), an industrial experience report on "a financial software under development for eight years," which "found that the size of tests grows much faster than of production code." Medium rather than high because this rests on one review, and the Sundelin finding reaches the corpus second-hand — the primary was never fetched. No primary source on test-suite maintenance, rework, or regression-suite upkeep cost is present in this corpus at all.
findings.citationCheck: supported (the claim lives in the PDF full text, not the arXiv abstract page)

findings.claim: The industrial studies that produce the largest reported benefits carry design defects that prevent causal attribution: non-equivalent comparison projects, unverified treatment, and post hoc single-team analysis.
findings.evidence: Non-equivalent comparators (Nagappan et al. 2008, Tables 1-2, read directly from the openly served table pages): MSN TDD project 26.0 source KLOC / 46 man-months / 5-8 developers versus a 'comparable project' of 149.0 KLOC / 144 man-months / 12 developers; Visual Studio 155.2 KLOC versus 222.0 KLOC; the same mismatch holds for the other pairs — a non-randomized, size-mismatched baseline underneath a per-KLOC defect ratio. Unverified treatment (same paper, Microsoft section): "There was no enforcement and monitoring of the TDD practice; and decisions to use TDD were made as a group" — so 'TDD' at the three Microsoft sites is an assumed rather than verified construct, and the paper concedes the Microsoft team "did most of their development using a hybrid version of TDD." (The paper draws this line itself: its IBM section states the opposite — "Complete unit testing was enforced.") Post hoc design (Sanchez et al. 2007): "we report on a post hoc analysis of the results of an IBM team" — one team, compared against its own pre-TDD project and an external industry benchmark, i.e. no randomization and no concurrent equivalent control. Confidence is medium, not high, because the conformance claim's blind citation audit came back UNREACHABLE (the Springer article body is paywalled; the abstract carries none of it); the sentence was verified verbatim by an adversarial verifier against an archived author PDF, and the claim's scope was corrected from 'the study' to specifically the three Microsoft sites.
findings.citationCheck: mixed — table/size claim SUPPORTED (tables served openly at the DOI); post hoc single-team claim SUPPORTED; conformance claim UNREACHABLE at the cited URL, restated here to the Microsoft sites only and flagged as verified against an archived copy rather than the cited page
findings.vote: 2-1 on each of the three component claims

findings.claim: The strongest genuinely longitudinal industrial data point in the corpus is a single IBM team sustaining TDD for five years across more than ten releases of a Java product.
findings.evidence: "an IBM team who has sustained use of TDD for five years and over ten releases of a Java-implemented product." This is the best case-FOR artifact available here, and it is weak in specific ways: n=1 team; post hoc rather than controlled; the team was selected precisely because it SUSTAINED TDD (selection on the outcome); two of three authors were IBM employees studying an IBM team; and the same IBM team appears in earlier work by overlapping authors, so this datapoint recurs in the literature as one team rather than several. The framing 'unusually long for TDD research' is a gloss on the literature, not a comparison the paper makes. Confidence is medium: single source, split vote, and only the abstract is publicly reachable.
findings.citationCheck: supported (verified via publisher metadata for the same DOI; IEEE Xplore bot-blocks direct fetching, so the abstract was recovered through Crossref/OpenAlex and an archived snapshot)

contradictions: EFFECT MAGNITUDE, and nothing adjudicates it: the industrial literature's headline — a 40-90% drop in pre-release defect density across four IBM/Microsoft teams — cannot be reconciled with a pooled controlled estimate that puts iterative test-last AHEAD of TDD by 7.06 percentage points. Critically, the claim carrying that 40-90% figure (with its paired 15-35% development-time increase) was REFUTED by the adversarial panel and is not carried into any finding above; the figure appears in this corpus only as abstract text quoted during citation auditing. So the contradiction survives in a degraded form: the surviving controlled evidence is null-to-reversed, and the industrial counterweight did not survive verification. Either the industrial comparators (MSN: 26.0 KLOC / 46 man-months versus 149.0 KLOC / 144 man-months) are measuring something other than TDD, or the lab proxies are measuring something other than defects. No source in the corpus settles this.

INDUSTRIAL COST STATEMENTS CONFLICT, and none of the quantitative ones survived: an IBM ISSRE 2003 assertion that 'productivity was not impacted', a meta-analytic finding that every industrial trial reported a productivity loss (mean -27%, smallest -15%), and Nagappan's 15-35% increase in initial development time cannot all be true of industrial TDD — and two of them are IBM. All three of those specific claims were refuted or never verified. What survives is only the weakest form: a 'moderate perceived' productivity loss with no measured effect size (Sanchez et al. 2007). Anyone quoting a percentage cost figure for TDD from this literature is quoting something this audit could not stand behind.

WHICH STUDIES ARE THE WEAK ONES — directly contested, unresolved. Munir et al. are reported to claim the no-difference findings come from LOW rigor/relevance studies that 'bias the results negatively' when pooled, implying methodological quality correlates with pro-TDD conclusions. Yet the most methodologically controlled work in this corpus — Fucci's process dissection, the 12-experiment multi-site family, repository mining with size-matched controls — is precisely what produces the nulls and reversals. Both accounts cannot stand. The claim stating Munir's rigor/relevance stratification was itself REFUTED by the panel, so this contradiction is flagged as live and unadjudicated rather than decided.

INDUSTRIAL SUBGROUP DATA — two syntheses appear to disagree about whether the data even exists: Rafique & Misic report an industrial subgroup showing both larger quality improvement and larger productivity drop, while another meta-analysis states that only ONE industrial study reported data adequate for a standardized effect size, and that its standardized results can therefore be trusted for academic studies only. Either Rafique's industrial subgroup rests on data the other says does not exist, or the two used incompatible inclusion/extraction rules. Neither claim survived verification; the corpus does not say which is right.

DIRECTION OF THE TEST-QUANTITY / DEFECT RELATION: repository-mining work reports a stable weak POSITIVE correlation between test-case count and recorded bugs (Spearman rho 0.25-0.417, p<2.2e-16, every year 2012-2021), corroborated by earlier mining work — the opposite sign to the entire pro-TDD case. These reconcile only if the mining proxy measures bug-fix commit ACTIVITY rather than escaped defects, a reconciliation the corpus gestures at but never establishes. These mining claims are among the 96 unverified and did not go through the panel, so treat the sign as unconfirmed in both directions.

CITATION MISMATCH ON THE CONFORMANCE EVIDENCE: the 2020 review cites Beller et al. as observing 2,443 developers over 2.5 years with 2.2% of test-containing sessions matching strict TDD, while the Beller primary in this corpus reports 416 developers over five months, 4% of test-containing sessions and 2% of developers. These cannot describe the same study, and the load-bearing conformance number differs by roughly a factor of two. Both Beller-derived claims were REFUTED by the panel, so no in-the-wild conformance percentage is asserted anywhere in the findings above — the conformance argument rests solely on Nagappan's own admission that TDD was not enforced or monitored at the Microsoft sites.

EFFECT MAGNITUDE: Nagappan et al. report a 40-90% drop in pre-release defect density across four IBM/Microsoft teams, while the random-effects pooled estimate for external quality is null (g=0.114, 95% CI -0.357 to 0.585, p=0.635) and the 12-experiment family finds iterative test-last AHEAD of TDD by 7.06 percentage points. An effect large enough to halve defect density should not vanish under controlled comparison; either the industrial comparators (MSN: 26.0 KLOC/46 man-months vs 149.0 KLOC/144 man-months) are measuring something other than TDD, or the lab proxies are measuring something other than defects. No source in the corpus adjudicates this.

INDUSTRIAL COST: Maximilien & Williams (IBM, ISSRE 2003) assert 'productivity was not impacted', but the thesis meta-analysis finds EVERY industrial trial reported a productivity loss (mean -27%, smallest -15%), Nagappan reports a 15-35% increase in initial development time at IBM and Microsoft, and Munir's high-rigor/high-relevance stratum finds the quality gain always accompanied by a productivity loss. These cannot all be true of industrial TDD, and two of them are IBM.

WHERE THE NULLS COME FROM: Munir et al. claim the no-difference findings come from the LOW rigor/relevance categories and that these 'bias the results negatively' when pooled — implying methodological quality correlates with pro-TDD conclusions. Yet the most methodologically controlled work in the corpus (Fucci's process dissection, the 12-experiment family with blinded/multi-site design, Borle's size-matched control sets) is precisely what produces the nulls and reversals. Both accounts of which studies are the weak ones cannot stand.

INDUSTRIAL SUBGROUP DATA: Rafique & Misic report a subgroup analysis showing industrial studies with BOTH larger quality improvement and larger productivity drop, whereas the thesis meta-analysis states that only ONE industrial study reported data adequate for a standardized effect size and that its standardized results can therefore be trusted for academic studies only. Either Rafique's industrial subgroup rests on data the other meta-analysis says does not exist, or the two used incompatible inclusion/extraction rules — and the corpus does not say which.

DIRECTION OF THE TEST-QUANTITY/DEFECT RELATION: Islam 2023 finds a stable weak POSITIVE correlation between test-case count and recorded bugs (Spearman rho 0.25-0.417, p<2.2e-16, every year 2012-2021), corroborating Kochhar 2013, while the entire pro-TDD case holds that more (and earlier) testing yields fewer defects. The two are reconcilable only if the mining proxy measures bug-fix commit ACTIVITY rather than escaped defects — a reconciliation the corpus gestures at but no source actually establishes.

CITATION MISMATCH ON BELLER: the 2020 review cites Beller et al. as observing 2,443 developers over 2.5 years with 2.2% of test-containing sessions matching strict TDD, while the Beller primary in the corpus reports 416 developers over five months, 4% of test-containing sessions, and 2% of developers. These figures cannot describe the same study — one of the two is a different paper or edition, and the load-bearing conformance number differs by roughly a factor of two.
caveats:
SCOPE OF VERIFICATION. Only 24 claims were eligible for verification and 11 survived; 96 lower-ranked claims were NEVER verified and contribute nothing to the findings above. Thirteen claims were REFUTED by the 3-lens panel and must not be quoted from this report: (1) the pooled external-quality effect g=0.30 fixed / 0.11 random across 9 trials and 434 subjects with I-squared 83.2; (2) the pooled productivity effect g=0.10 fixed / 0.07 random across 8 trials and 153 subjects; (3) the setting moderator reversing productivity sign (+11% academia, -27% industry, every industrial trial a loss, smallest 15%) — all three killed on counter-evidence and provenance grounds at the same thesis source; (4) the claim that conformance was essentially unmeasured across the pre-2011 corpus; (5) the claim that the 12-experiment family's authors state no empirical TDD study checks treatment conformance; (6) the two in-the-wild conformance measurements (Beller 2.2% of sessions; Borle 0.8% of 256,572 GitHub projects); (7) the review's claim that iteration degree matters more than test-first ordering; (8) the Munir rigor/relevance stratification result; (9) the claim that TDD's apparent superiority stems from comparing against coarse-grained waterfall controls; (10) the Nagappan headline of 40-90% pre-release defect-density reduction at 15-35% added development time with the time figure labelled 'subjective'; (11) the claim that Nagappan's Table 3 annotates that figure as '[Management estimates]'; (12) the characterization of Sanchez's baseline as a non-equivalent historical project plus industry benchmark; (13) the Munir abstract-level claim that high-rigor/high-relevance studies show quality improvement accompanied by productivity loss. Several of these are the figures most commonly cited in practitioner arguments about TDD, in both directions.

UNANSWERED SUB-QUESTIONS. One of eight coverage areas is entirely UNANSWERED: TDD's defect-removal yield per hour against alternative uses of the same time (code review/inspection, static analysis, property-based testing, CI), generalization to current practice, and falsification criteria for either side — nothing at all was gathered. Six more are PARTIAL: the proxy-versus-field-defect comparison cannot be completed because no source in the corpus measures post-release or customer-reported defects; synthesis coverage lacks Bissi et al. 2016 and any post-2018 systematic review, and primary-study pool overlap between the meta-analyses is asserted but never enumerated, so their apparent agreement may not be independent corroboration; lifecycle cost rests on one second-hand mention; industrial coverage is missing Ericsson/Nokia long-term adoption studies and every regulated-domain (medical device, avionics) report; publication bias, researcher allegiance and statistical power have ZERO evidence in either direction (no funnel plot, Egger test, or power analysis was located); longitudinal in-industry adoption data is nearly absent, standing on one five-year case study.

SOURCE WEAKNESSES. Two of the three industrial sources are substantially vendor self-reports: Nagappan and Bhat were Microsoft employees, Maximilien was at IBM, and Sanchez et al. is two IBM authors studying an IBM team — the defect and effort figures are internally collected and not independently audited. Both are paywalled, so parts of this analysis rest on archived author PDFs and openly served table pages rather than the cited article body; the conformance claim's blind audit came back UNREACHABLE rather than supported and has been restated to the Microsoft sites only. The controlled-experiment evidence runs almost entirely on TDD novices and toy tasks; the one professional-subject study (39 professionals, 82 data points) is correlational regression, not a randomized test-first/test-last contrast. Fucci et al.'s ESEM 2016 blind-analysis multi-site replication was never fetched as a primary.

TIME SENSITIVITY. The primary sources date to 2007, 2008, 2016 and 2020. For claims about study design (post hoc, single team, table figures) age is irrelevant — those facts do not decay. For the empirical question they do age: no synthesis after 2018 was retrieved, and the corpus predates any effect that modern CI, mandatory code review, LLM-assisted test generation, or current tooling would have on the trade-off. One incidental note in the corpus flags that a 2013 mining sample predates mandatory review and CI. Treat 'no demonstrated effect of test-first ordering' as the state of a 2007-2020 record, not as a settled finding about 2026 practice.
openQuestions: Does TDD change post-release or customer-reported defect rates at all? Not one source in this corpus measures it. Every surviving quality result is an experimenter-built oracle pass rate, a functional-correctness score on an assigned task, or an in-house pre-release defect density against a non-equivalent comparator. The literal question — production defects — has no direct evidence behind it in either direction.

What does a TDD-generated test suite cost over a product's life? The only signal is one eight-year industrial report, reached second-hand, finding test code grows much faster than production code, alongside a 2020 review's finding that no study on managing those tests exists. Whether that growth represents compounding maintenance debt or amortized safety is unstudied.

If the active ingredient is granularity and uniformity rather than test-first ordering, does an equally fine-grained non-TDD process (iterative test-last with enforced small steps) capture the same benefit at lower cost? The 12-experiment family's ITL comparison is suggestive but not designed to answer this, and no study in the corpus manipulates step size independently of test ordering.

How does TDD's defect-removal yield per hour compare with the alternatives competing for the same hours — code review, static analysis, property-based testing, stronger CI? Nothing was gathered on any alternative, so 'TDD versus nothing' is the only comparison this literature supports, and it is not the comparison an engineering manager actually faces.

coverage.subQuestion: 1. VERIFY THE PREMISE: do defect-reduction studies measure production/post-release defects or lab proxies, and does effect direction/size differ between the two classes?
coverage.note: Classification is done and the answer is stark (acceptance-test pass rate, in-house verification defects/KLOC, bug-fix-commit regexes) — but the comparison the sub-question asks for cannot be completed because NOT ONE source in the corpus measures clean post-release/customer-reported field defects, and no source explicitly states that gap, so the 'production-defect study' arm is empty rather than measured.

coverage.subQuestion: 2. Pooled effect sizes, CIs, heterogeneity and moderators from the meta-analyses/systematic reviews, and how much their primary-study pools overlap (so agreement is not independent corroboration)?
coverage.note: Full numeric pooling (g, CI, Q, I-squared) exists only for one thesis meta-analysis; Rafique & Misic 2013 and Munir 2014 are captured qualitatively with no pooled g or CI; Bissi et al. 2016 is entirely absent, no post-2018 synthesis has been retrieved, and study-pool overlap is asserted ('largely overlapping') but never enumerated study-by-study.

coverage.subQuestion: 3. Measured cost in developer time as effect sizes with dispersion, and does ANY study measure lifecycle cost (maintenance, rework, regression-suite upkeep) rather than initial implementation only?
coverage.note: Initial-effort cost is well covered with dispersion (g=0.10/0.07 n.s., I-squared 82.9; -27% industrial mean, every industrial trial a loss, smallest 15%; Nagappan's 15-35% flagged as management estimate) — but the lifecycle half rests entirely on one second-hand mention of Sundelin et al. inside the 2020 review; no primary source on test-suite maintenance, rework, or regression upkeep cost has been fetched.

coverage.subQuestion: 4. VERIFY THE CONSTRUCT: is TDD operationalized consistently, does benefit survive isolating test-FIRST from granularity/uniformity/test-effort/refactoring, and how many studies measured conformance?
coverage.note: Converged from four independent angles (Fucci dissection: sequencing has no important influence, granularity/uniformity do; the 12-experiment family: ITL ahead by 7.06pp; Beller: 2-4% strict conformance, 12% of self-reported TDD projects verified; Borle: 0.8% of 256,572 repos); only gap is that Fucci et al.'s ESEM 2016 blind-analysis multi-site replication was not fetched as a primary.

coverage.subQuestion: 5. Strongest INDUSTRIAL evidence (Microsoft/IBM, IBM Retail, Ericsson, regulated medical/avionics) and the internal-validity threats constraining each?
coverage.note: Nagappan 2008, Sanchez/IBM Retail 2007 and Maximilien & Williams 2003 are captured with their threats itemized (non-equivalent size-mismatched comparators, historical baselines, self-selection, unmeasured conformance) — but Ericsson/Nokia long-term adoption studies and every regulated-domain (medical device, avionics) report are missing, and researcher-allegiance/publication-by-advocates is named as a threat with no evidence gathered on it.

coverage.subQuestion: 6. WHAT EXPLAINS THE DISAGREEMENT: which candidate causes are empirically supported as moderators by subgroup/meta-regression versus merely asserted?
coverage.note: Four moderators are empirically supported (setting, task size, test-effort difference, rigor/relevance stratification) and one is empirically refuted as sufficient (participant type — both subgroup CIs cross zero with residual heterogeneity), but control-condition choice (waterfall vs ITL) is only asserted, never meta-regressed, and publication bias, researcher allegiance and statistical power have zero evidence in either direction — no funnel plot, Egger test or power analysis has been located.

coverage.subQuestion: 7. Large-scale observational evidence — repository mining and longitudinal in-industry adoption — and the confounds specific to that method?
coverage.note: The mining half is strong (Borle's null on all five outcomes with matched controls; Islam 2023 and Kochhar 2013 on test count vs bug count; confounds itemized: commit-order inference, 79%-precision bug regex, control set drawn only from repos that already have tests, language mis-detection, size/team co-variation) — but longitudinal in-industry adoption data is essentially absent, with only Sanchez's 5-year IBM case study and a second-hand Sundelin mention standing in for it.

coverage.subQuestion: 8. COMPARATIVE AND BOUNDARY CONDITIONS: TDD's defect-removal yield per hour against review/static analysis/property-based testing/CI, generalization to current practice, and falsification criteria for both sides?
coverage.note: Nothing gathered on any alternative use of the same hours — no inspection/review effectiveness data, no static-analysis or property-based-testing comparison, no per-hour defect-removal yield for anything; the only touch on baseline drift is an incidental note that Kochhar's 2013 sample predates mandatory review/CI, and no falsification criteria for either the pro or the against case have been sourced.

citationDetail.claim: This 12-experiment family measures 'quality' as a lab proxy, not production or post-release defects: external quality is the percentage of experimenter-written acceptance/oracle tests passed on toy tasks (MR and BSK), which participants never saw. So its findings bear on proxy-outcome studies, not on field defect rates.
citationDetail.reasoning: Every component of the statement is verbatim in the cited paper (Santos et al., A Family of Experiments on Test-Driven Development, arXiv:2011.11942), fetched at https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.11942 and its PDF at the same identifier (/tmp/claude-1000/-home-<user>-Desktop-Lab/9e11ce5a-30c7-475c-b67a-0bb78a03d4c7/scratchpad/p.txt). 1. 12-experiment family — the landing-page abstract states: We conduct a family of 12 experiments on TDD in academia and industry. We aggregate their results by means of meta-analysis. 2. external quality is the percentage of experimenter-written acceptance/oracle tests passed — Section 3.1: The main response variable (dependent variable) within the family is external quality. As usual in the TDD literature, we measure external quality as the percentage of successful tests in the test battery—or test oracle—that we (i.e., the experimenters) built to test participant solutions. Also §1: we define quality as the percentage of test battery tests developed by the experimenters that pass. The formula given is QLTY = #Tests(Pass)/#Tests(All) * 100%. 3. which participants never saw — The participants had no access to these test oracles. 4. toy tasks (MR and BSK) — the paper's own wording: TDD and ITL were applied by the participants in our experiments to develop at least one out of five toy tasks: MarsRover (MR), Bowling Scorekeeper (BSK), MusicPhone (MP), Sudoku (SDK) and Spread-Sheet (SS). The GQM statement likewise scopes it: in the context of TDD novices coding toy tasks in controlled experiments. Table 2 gives the oracle sizes (MR 52 tests, BSK 48). 5. not production or post-release defects... bears on proxy-outcome studies, not on field defect rates — this is the report author's framing rather than a sentence in the paper, but it follows with no interpretive leap: the sole response variable is oracle-test pass rate on toy tasks in controlled experiments (the paper's own GQM), and the word defect appears nowhere in the paper; no field or post-release outcome is measured or claimed. Two minor caveats that do not change the verdict: (a) the statement names only MR and BSK, while the family used five toy tasks — though the paper itself sets aside MP, SDK and SS (Regarding RQ2, we consider the data of MR and BSK only. The participants in the experiments of our family were seldom set the SDK, MP and SS tasks), and all five are described as toy tasks, so the characterization holds; (b) the operationalization detail lives in the full text, not in the landing page's truncated abstract — under a strict abstract-page-text-only reading this would be partial, but the PDF is served from the same arXiv identifier the citation names, and it states each claim verbatim.

citationDetail.claim: Pooling all 12 experiments in a random-effects meta-analysis, iterative test-last (ITL) beat TDD on external quality by 7.06 percentage points (95% CI -14.47 to 0.35) — a non-significant effect in the direction OPPOSITE to the pro-TDD claim — with medium heterogeneity (I-squared = 67.8%, Q = 39.70, p < 0.001).
citationDetail.reasoning: The cited arXiv item is Santos et al., A Family of Experiments on Test-Driven Development (arXiv:2011.11942). Every element of the statement checks out against the paper. The /abs/ landing page itself carries the abstract, which independently confirms the qualitative core: We conduct a family of 12 experiments on TDD in academia and industry. We aggregate their results by means of meta-analysis... TDD novices achieve a slightly higher code quality with iterative test-last development (i.e., ITL, the reverse approach of TDD) than with TDD. The specific figures live in Section 4.2 of the same arXiv paper (verified via the ar5iv full-text rendering of the identical arXiv ID, then grepped for each number in the raw source). Each maps exactly: - iterative test-last (ITL) beat TDD... by 7.06 percentage points -> ITL achieves higher quality than TDD (M=-7.06). The sign is negative because the estimate is TDD minus ITL; the paper's own prose reads it as ITL ahead. The report converts this retrieval failure into a substantive finding ("the cost side ... is an argument, not a measurement"). The user asked "what does it cost in development time"; the report answers "nobody knows," which the pool does not establish.

Checklist item 7 produced zero claims. Borle et al.'s GitHub study — named in the scope — is absent, as is all other large-N repository-mining evidence and all longitudinal in-industry adoption data. An entire assigned perspective (Repository data auditor) returned nothing and the report does not say so. This is the sharpest gap: repository mining links commit-inferred test-first patterns to issue-tracker defects, i.e. it is the one retrieved method that could have spoken to the report's own headline complaint that no study measures field defects.

Checklist item 8 produced zero claims. No defect-removal-efficiency figures for code inspection, static analysis, property-based/fuzz testing, or integration-level test-after; no assessment of whether pre-CI-era baselines still hold under mandatory review, modern static analysis, or LLM-assisted coding. A reader deciding whether to spend the hours on TDD or on review gets no denominator at all.

Checklist item 8's explicit deliverable — "State what evidence would falsify the pro case and what would falsify the against case" — appears nowhere in the executive summary or in any of the seven findings.

Checklist item 5's named industrial sources beyond Microsoft/IBM are all missing: Ericsson, regulated medical-device and avionics reports, and IBM Retail/Sanchez as a distinct study. The report's phrase "the industrial studies that motivate adoption" rests on two papers.
Publication bias and researcher allegiance (checklist items 2 and 6) were never assessed — no funnel plot, no allegiance coding, no discussion. Zero claims in the pool touch either.

Recency: the newest dated item in the pool is a 2020 review. Nothing from 2021-2026, despite the scope explicitly asking for post-2018 syntheses and for whether the baselines generalise to current practice including LLM-assisted coding.

Source types never touched: (a) primary-paper headline RESULTS — from Nagappan et al. and the IBM paper the audit extracted only methodological defects ([6], [7], [8]) and never the effects being criticised; (b) any replication package or dataset; (c) any dissenting or pro-TDD expert response to Fucci's dissection or to the Santos et al. family; (d) any non-English or non-Western source; (e) large-N practitioner field telemetry linking test-first practice to change-failure rate (DORA/Accelerate-style survey data), which is the only existing large-sample field-outcome source on this question.

Corpus size is never disclosed. Eleven claims spanning roughly four to five distinct papers underwrite a verdict about the entire empirical literature. Nowhere does the report separate "the literature contains no production-defect evidence" from "this retrieval found none" — the two are collapsed in the first sentence of the summary and in Finding 1.

Checklist item 2 (meta-analyses) produced ZERO claims. Not one pooled effect size, confidence interval, I-squared, funnel-plot test, or moderator regression from Turhan et al. 2010, Rafique & Misic 2013, Munir et al. 2014, Bissi et al. 2016, or any post-2018 synthesis reached the pool — despite the scoper naming all four by author and year. The report's headline ('where the comparison is controlled and pooled, TDD does not win') rests on a single experiment family while the four canonical pooled syntheses were never retrieved. Rafique & Misic in particular reports a small-to-moderate quality benefit that is larger in industrial than academic settings; its absence is not neutral, it is the missing counterweight.

The overlap question the scoper explicitly posed — 'to what extent do they pool the same overlapping primary studies (so that agreement between reviews is not independent corroboration)' — was never answered, because no review was retrieved at all.

Checklist item 6 (WHAT EXPLAINS THE DISAGREEMENT) is unanswered end to end. The pool contains no subgroup or meta-regression evidence separating empirically supported moderators (student vs. professional, control = test-last vs. unstructured, task duration, outcome metric, conformance) from merely asserted ones. [1] reports I-squared = 67.8% — i.e., real heterogeneity exists — and nothing in the report explains a single source of it. The user's question asked directly: 'Where studies disagree, explain what accounts for the disagreement.' The report does not.

Checklist item 7 (repository mining) produced ZERO claims. Borle et al.'s GitHub analysis — named in the scope, and the only large-N observational evidence class in the plan — is entirely absent, as is any longitudinal in-industry adoption data. An entire method family that would have tested the lab findings at scale was dropped without acknowledgement.

Checklist item 8 (comparative yield and boundary conditions) produced ZERO claims. No defect-removal-per-hour comparison against code review/inspection, static analysis, property-based testing, or CI investment; no assessment of whether pre-CI-era baselines generalize; and no statement of what evidence would falsify the pro case or the against case, which the scoper committed to state explicitly.

The pro-side effect magnitudes were never retrieved. The pool has critiques of Nagappan et al. and the IBM team ([6]-[9]) but not one number they reported. A reader cannot judge whether a 'size-mismatched comparator' undermines a 40% defect reduction or a 4% one. This makes the 'strongest honest case FOR' structurally unbuildable from the pool.

Checklist item 4's designated decisive test is only half-covered. [3]/[4]/[5] are the dissection paper; Fucci et al.'s blinded, multi-site external replication — the scoper's stated gold standard — contributed no claim. Nor was the count the scoper asked for ('how many studies measured process conformance at all') ever produced: [6] covers Microsoft alone.

Checklist item 5's regulated-industry evidence is entirely missing: no Ericsson report, no medical-device (IEC 62304) or avionics (DO-178C) case data, despite these being the settings where post-release defect telemetry is most rigorously collected — exactly the outcome measure the report says is unavailable.

No source newer than ~2020/2021 appears in the pool. Today is 2026; five years of subsequent measurement, including anything on TDD under LLM-assisted coding (which the scoper's item 8 explicitly asked about), was never searched.

Source types never searched at all: systematic-review primary papers; any MSR dataset or replication package; any non-English or non-Western industrial report; any defect-tracking or field-telemetry dataset; and any evidence-positive methodologist who would defend the pooled pro-quality estimates.
planFlaws: The six perspectives share one blind spot: every one is defined by what it distrusts ("distrusts vote-counting narratives," "distrusts the TDD construct itself," "distrusts university experiments," "distrusts any 'quality improved' finding," "distrusts self-reported adherence," "distrusts single-intervention studies"). No perspective was tasked with assembling the strongest evidence-based case FOR TDD from primary sources. The result is visible in the pool: eleven claims, not one of which reports a positive effect of any magnitude. The user asked for "the strongest honest case both for and against"; the perspective set made the pro side unreachable, and the for-case the report actually produces is that one team kept doing it for five years.

Sub-question 4 pre-designates its own answer: "Fucci et al.'s dissection and blinded multi-site replication work is the decisive test here." Naming a paper decisive before retrieval guarantees the synthesis inherits its conclusion. Finding 3 is [high] confidence resting entirely on that one correlational analysis of 82 data points from 39 professionals, with no replication in the pool — and the "blinded multi-site replication" half of the sub-question returned nothing at all.

Sub-questions 1 and 4 are framed as instructions to find fault ("VERIFY THE PREMISE," "VERIFY THE CONSTRUCT") rather than to measure. Item 1's proxy-vs-production binary disqualifies every lab study a priori; combined with a retrieval that found no production-defect study, it made the conclusion "the record cannot answer the question" near-inevitable independent of what the studies showed.

The scope accepted "studies disagree" as a premise (item 6 asks what explains the disagreement) but the retrieval returned only one side of it. The disagreement was therefore never characterised, and the report presents a one-sided corpus in the register of a settled state of evidence.

Heterogeneity was requested (item 2), obtained (I-squared 67.8%, Q = 39.70, p < 0.001 in [1]), quoted — and then not used. A pooled estimate with substantial heterogeneity and a CI crossing zero supports "the effect varies widely by setting and cannot be pinned down here," not the report's "TDD does not win." No subgroup or moderator analysis was run on the one dataset in the pool that carried the statistics to support it.

No step in the plan required extracting each primary study's reported RESULT alongside its methodological defects. The pool shows the asymmetry cleanly: from Nagappan et al. the audit took Table 2's comparator sizes and the conformance gap, but not the paper's defect-density or effort findings. A reader cannot see what is being rebutted and so cannot judge whether the caveats are large enough to overturn the effects.

The plan set no corpus-adequacy floor and no escalation rule. Sub-questions 3, 7 and 8 returned no claims whatsoever, and the pipeline neither re-searched nor surfaced the shortfall anywhere in the deliverable.

All six perspectives are defined by what they DISTRUST. Read their briefs: 'distrusts vote-counting narratives', 'distrusts the TDD construct itself', 'distrusts university experiments... and equally distrusts vendor case studies', 'distrusts any quality-improved finding', 'distrusts self-reported adherence', 'distrusts single-intervention studies'. No perspective was assigned to build the strongest pro-TDD case from primary evidence. The claim pool that resulted is 9 debunks out of 11 claims, and the summary's pro case is a duration fact plus a mechanism. The question asked for 'the strongest honest case both for and against'; the perspective set made the FOR case unreachable by construction. This is a shared blind spot, not six independent viewpoints.

Sub-question 1 is written as 'VERIFY THE PREMISE' with the failure mode pre-loaded ('or lab proxies... a toy task'). It is a leading sub-question, and it consumed the answer: the report's top-line conclusion is the premise-failure verdict, and the six other checklist items that would have qualified it went unretrieved.

The report converts a RETRIEVAL failure into a claim about the STATE OF THE EVIDENCE. 'The retrieved empirical record does not answer the question as posed' is defensible; Finding 1's 'The premise of the question is not testable against this evidence base' at [high] confidence is not, when the four named systematic reviews and the entire repository-mining literature were never searched. A user acting on this would reasonably conclude no production-defect evidence for TDD exists.

No stopping rule tied coverage to the checklist. Four of eight committed sub-questions (2, 6, 7, 8) yielded zero claims, yet the report proceeds to a confident global verdict without a limitations section naming which sub-questions returned nothing. The reader cannot tell the difference between 'searched and found null' and 'never searched'.

The scoper correctly identified non-independent corroboration as a threat (item 2) but built no defense against its mirror image, and the synthesis walked straight into it: one experiment family, one research group, two shared tasks (MR/BSK per [0]) is treated as 'the controlled and pooled evidence' for the entire field.

Item 3 asks for cost 'as effect sizes with dispersion rather than a single headline percentage' — a good instruction that, unmet, left the report with nothing at all on cost except [10]'s 'perceived' and 'moderate'. The plan had no fallback for the case where the preferred evidence grade does not exist: the correct output there is 'the commonly cited figures are X, sourced from non-randomized study Y', not silence, since the user explicitly asked what TDD costs in development time and the report effectively answers 'unknown' without saying what the field currently claims and why it is weak.
rationales: A reader acting on this report would conclude that the empirical record shows TDD does not reduce defects and that its cost has never been measured. Neither is established by the claim pool. The pool covers roughly four to five papers; every named meta-analysis in the scoper's own checklist is absent, all repository-mining evidence is absent, all comparative/opportunity-cost evidence is absent, and no effort effect size was retrieved — including from a paper the audit demonstrably had open (Nagappan et al., quoted at Table 2). The report converts these retrieval failures into substantive findings at high confidence, and its first sentence (every study whose citation survived audit measures a proxy) is contradicted by claim [7]'s own reference to a per-KLOC defect ratio in shipped industrial projects. Two structural plan defects produced this: a perspective set in which all six lenses are adversarial, so no positive effect estimate was ever sought, and a sub-question that named one paper the decisive test before retrieval began. Secondary but concrete: the single quantitative headline prints a point estimate (7.06) that falls outside its own quoted CI (-14.47 to 0.35), findings 5 and 7 each call a different study the one longitudinal data point, and the summary's pro-case rests on a study duration with no reported outcome.

Two independent failures each reach the material threshold. (1) Traceability: the summary's opening sentence and Finding 1 assert at high confidence that EVERY surviving study measures a lab proxy rather than production defects, which the pool contradicts — claim [7] explicitly describes a per-KLOC defect ratio on shipped Microsoft products, and [8]/[9] describe an IBM product across 10+ releases. The report critiques the internal validity of industrial defect-density studies and then reclassifies them as proxy studies. Compounding this, the entire pro side of the summary rests on a fact ([9], five years of sustained adoption) that says nothing about outcomes, and on 'lifecycle cost has never been measured', an absolute the hedged claim [2] does not license. (2) Coverage: four of eight committed sub-questions — the meta-analyses, the disagreement analysis, the repository-mining evidence, and the comparative/falsifiability analysis — produced zero claims, and the report never says so. The user's own question ('explain what accounts for the disagreement', 'what does it cost in development time') is therefore answered with a heterogeneity statistic and no moderators, and with one 'perceived, moderate' qualitative remark. A practitioner reading this would conclude the empirical case for TDD is empty; what is actually empty is the retrieval. The individual verified claims are accurately quoted — the numbers in [1] and [7] are reproduced correctly and the hedge in [4] survives — so the failure is in generalization and in silence about what was never searched, not in fabrication.

refuted.claim: The pooled standardized effect of TDD on external quality was small and lost statistical significance under a random-effects model: g = 0.30 (fixed) vs g = 0.11 (random) across 9 trials and 434 subjects, with high heterogeneity (Table 3.3 gives fixed 0.301, 95% CI 0.133–0.470, p=0.000; random 0.114, 95% CI −0.357–0.585, p=0.635; Q=47.718, I²=83.2, df=8, p=0.000).
refuted.why: The numbers transcribe correctly (I downloaded the thesis PDF from figshare file 28143561 and confirmed Table 3.3 verbatim: OVERALL 9 / fixed 0.301, 0.133–0.470, p=0.000 / random 0.114, −0.357–0.585, p=0.635, Q=47.718, I²=83.235, df=8). But the claim is superseded and materially misrepresents its own source on three independent grounds. (1) SUPERSEDED BY THE SAME AUTHORS' PEER-REVIEWED VERSION. This is an unrefereed 2011 MSc thesis (Yahya Rafique, supervisor Vojislav Mišić). The same author-supervisor pair published the finished work as Rafique & Mišić, The Effects of Test-Driven Development on External Quality and Productivity: A Meta-Analysis, IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 39(6):835–856, 2013, DOI 10.1109/TSE.2012.28 (127 citations; confirmed via OpenAlex and Crossref). It covers 27 studies, not 9 trials, and concludes TDD has a small positive effect on external quality with little to no discernible effect on productivity — and that industrial studies showed substantially larger quality gains. Citing the 9-trial thesis table as the state of the meta-analytic evidence quotes the preliminary draft over the refereed, three-times-larger final measurement. (2) EXACT OVERREACH — the claim calls this the pooled standardized effect of TDD on external quality, but the thesis disqualifies it from that reading. §3.2.2.3, p.34: Only one of the studies conducted in industry reported data adequate for standardized effect size calculation. Accordingly, the standardized analysis can only be trusted with respect to academic studies. The g=0.30/0.11 figure is an academic-student-only estimate that structurally excludes industrial settings — i.e. exactly the production software context the research question asks about, and the subgroup where the same author later found the effect largest. (3) CONTRADICTED BY THE SOURCE'S OWN COMPANION ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSION. In the same chapter, §3.2.2.2 reports an unstandardized analysis over 18 trials / 571 subjects (double the trials, 32% more subjects) finding a mean 28% improvement in quality, with 12/18 trials above +10% and only one trial reporting a drop. And the thesis's own Discussion, §3.3 p.49, states: The summary effect sizes in our meta-analysis suggest that TDD has a small to medium sized overall positive effect on quality and a very small to negligible negative effect on productivity. The claim's framing (small and lost statistical significance) inverts the valence of the author's own stated bottom line by quoting the narrower of two parallel analyses and omitting the wider one. Caveat on method: WebSearch and Tavily budgets were exhausted before I ran, so the negation/critique searches were done via Semantic Scholar, Crossref, OpenAlex APIs and direct retrieval of the primary PDF rather than general web search. That was sufficient to establish supersession and misrepresentation, but I did not survey post-2016 critiques (e.g. Bissi et al. 2016, ISWC/IST DOI 10.1016/j.infsof.2016.02.004, surfaced but unread) that might qualify further.

refuted.claim: The pooled standardized effect of TDD on productivity was statistically indistinguishable from zero: g = 0.10 (fixed) and 0.07 (random) across only 8 trials / 153 subjects, both non-significant at .05, with significant high heterogeneity (Table 3.5: fixed 95% CI −0.208–0.401, p=0.536; random 95% CI −0.688–0.829, p=0.856; Q=40.949, I²=82.9).
refuted.why: SUPERSEDED BY THE SAME AUTHORS' PEER-REVIEWED VERSION OF RECORD, AND MATERIALLY QUALIFIED BY IT. 1) Provenance/supersession defect. The claim rests on Yahya Rafique's unpublished Ryerson MSc thesis TDD Dynamics (figshare DOI 10.32920/ryerson.14661051; figshare metadata confirms defined_type = Thesis, Master of Science, published_date 2011-01-01, posted 2021-05-24). The same author with his supervisor published the meta-analysis as Rafique, Y. & Misic, V. B., The Effects of Test-Driven Development on External Quality and Productivity: A Meta-Analysis, IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 39(6):835-856, 2013, DOI 10.1109/TSE.2012.28 — verified independently via Crossref, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar (127 cited-by in OpenAlex, 124 in Semantic Scholar). The published version pools **27 studies**. The claim cites the student draft's 8 trials / 153 subjects as if it were the state of the evidence. When a peer-reviewed journal meta-analysis by the identical authors covering 27 studies exists, quoting the thesis's Table 3.5 is citing the draft over the version of record. 2) Direct material contradiction of the substantive conclusion. The TSE 2013 abstract (reconstructed from OpenAlex abstract_inverted_index) reads: The results indicate that, in general, TDD has a small positive effect on quality but little to no discernible effect on productivity. However, subgroup analysis has found both quality improvement and **productivity drop** to be much larger in industrial studies in comparison with academic studies. So the successor analysis does NOT report a flat null on productivity — it reports a pooled near-null that decomposes into an appreciable productivity DROP in industrial settings. Since the research question asks specifically about production software and what it costs in development time, the industrial subgroup is the relevant estimate and the pooled g=0.10/0.07 inverts the answer for that population. 3) Internal scope overreach in the quote itself. The supporting text says For the **standardized** analysis on productivity, effect sizes were computed for eight trials — i.e. 8 trials/153 subjects is one analysis stream in the thesis (unstandardized analyses covered a different, larger set), not the thesis's productivity evidence base. The claim presents a subset as the whole. The claim's own reported heterogeneity (Q=40.949, I^2=82.9, ~83% of variance between-study) means the pooled figure is not interpretable as one common effect, which is exactly what the 2013 subgroup analysis went on to demonstrate. Verification limit, stated honestly: WebSearch budget for the session was exhausted (200/200) and Tavily returned plan-limit errors, so I could not run the negation searches; IEEE Xplore and the figshare article page returned 403. I therefore confirmed authorship, year, venue, study count and the subgroup clause through three independent bibliographic APIs, but could NOT retrieve the exact industrial-subgroup effect size or CI from the TSE paper. The supersession and the qualifying subgroup finding are established; the precise magnitude of the industrial productivity drop is not.

refuted.claim: Setting is an empirically observed moderator that reverses the sign of the productivity result: in the unstandardized analysis (10 academic + 5 industrial trials) mean productivity improvement was +11% in academia but −27% in industry, and every single industrial trial reported a productivity loss, the smallest being 15%.
refuted.why: Counter-evidence found on four fronts. (1) The source's own weighted analysis contradicts the claim's headline. I pulled the full thesis PDF (figshare file 28143561, Rafique_Yahha.pdf) and read §3.2.3. Its standardized (effect-size) productivity meta-analysis reports g=0.096 fixed (p=.536) and 0.070 random (p=.856) — statistically insignificant — and states verbatim: the standardized analysis on productivity only utilized data from one industrial trial. Hence, the results can only be trusted to illustrate the productivity-related performance of TDD in the academic sector. The industrial subgroup in the properly weighted analysis is literally n=1 (Canfora et al., g=-1.111), so the source cannot support setting is an empirically observed moderator in any weighted sense; only the unstandardized raw-percentage arithmetic produces the +11%/-27% split, and the thesis itself warns of that measure that there is a possibility that the effect is exaggerated and that the data in the studies included here—esp. those in the industrial group—is insufficient. (2) A peer-reviewed source contradicts the moderator attribution. Fucci et al., An External Replication on the Effects of Test-driven Development Using a Multi-site Blind Analysis Approach, ESEM 2016 (DOI 10.1145/2961111.2962592, full text bura.brunel.ac.uk/bitstream/2438/13448/1/FullText.pdf), summarizing the published journal version of this very meta-analysis (Rafique & Mišić, IEEE TSE 2013, DOI 10.1109/TSE.2012.28, 27 primary studies): The results, based on effect sizes, do not show solid evidence either in support, or against, TDD... TDD improves external quality of 24% with respect to a waterfall approach; however, its effects are detrimental (-13%) when compared to an iterative test-last (ITL) approach... Conversely, TDD increases productivity—27% vis-à-vis ITL, and 7% vis-à-vis waterfall development. The sign flips the published version emphasizes are driven by the CONTROL technique, not by setting. (3) The universal every single industrial trial reported a productivity loss is contradicted by a prior review the thesis itself summarizes: Siniaalto's review of 13 studies — With regard to productivity, studies within the industrial and semi-industrial groups reported all possible outcomes, while the results from the academic group were limited to non-negative impact (thesis §2). Turhan et al.'s review, also summarized there, reports productivity results that are inconsistent across study types. (4) Composition and arithmetic defects in the 5-trial industrial subgroup. I reconstructed the partition from Table 3.6 by brute force: the only reading consistent with both reported means and the thesis's own Table 3.2 list of industrial studies is industrial = {Canfora -57, Bhat & Nagappan T1 -30, Williams et al. -18, George & Williams -16, Bhat & Nagappan T2 -15} (mean -27.2) and academic = the remaining ten (mean 11.4) — which means a sixth industrial trial in the same table, Nagappan et al. (-23%), was silently dropped from both subgroups (16 trials in Table 3.6, only 10+5=15 in the subgroup analysis). Those five are not five independent industrial projects: Bhat & Nagappan T1/T2 are two teams from one Microsoft case-study paper and Nagappan et al. 2008 re-reports the same Microsoft/IBM teams as Williams et al.; and per the thesis's own Table 3.2, George & Williams is a 5-hour, 200-LOC bowling-scorekeeper kata (24 subjects) and Canfora a 10-hour task — short lab exercises with professionals, not production delivery. Setting is also fully confounded with task size and duration in this data (academic trials ~450 LOC katas vs industrial 6,000–155,200 LOC, thousands of hours), and the thesis concedes programs implemented in the academic studies were generally much smaller in size in comparison with programs implemented in the industrial studies. (5) Superseded: post-2011 measurements find no setting-dependent productivity sign — Fucci et al. 2016 replication (p=.83 for productivity, negligible Cliff's δ=0.14), Baldassarre et al. 2021 (arXiv 2105.03312) We observed that TDD affects neither the external quality of software products nor developers' productivity, and Santos et al., A family of experiments on test-driven development, EMSE 2021 (DOI 10.1007/s10664-020-09895-8, arXiv 2011.11942), 12 experiments spanning academia and industry. The defensible residue is narrow: in this 2011 unstandardized snapshot, the five (non-independent, partly kata-based) industrial trials all showed raw productivity drops of 15–57%; that is not the same as setting is an empirically observed moderator that reverses the sign.

refuted.claim: Process conformance was essentially unmeasured in the pre-2011 TDD corpus: the meta-analysis reports that few of the analyzed studies gave explicit details on actual conformance levels or on steps taken to enforce conformance, so treatment groups were assumed rather than verified to be doing TDD.
refuted.why: Three unlicensed moves between quote and claim. (1) Reporting gap → measurement gap. Quote: few studies provided explicit details on actual conformance levels or on any steps that were taken to ensure a higher degree of conformance. That is a statement about what studies *reported*. The claim converts it into Process conformance was essentially unmeasured and, in the clause it appends with so, into treatment groups were assumed rather than verified to be doing TDD. Absence of reported detail is not evidence that no measurement or verification occurred; the quote's own wording (explicit details on actual conformance levels) presupposes conformance levels existed and that some studies did report them. The so… assumed rather than verified clause is an inference the source sentence does not make and is the load-bearing part of the claim. (2) Scope widened. The quote is scoped to studies in which subjects in a group were instructed to utilize a particular development process — i.e. the subject-based experiments this work analyzed. The claim restates it as a property of the pre-2011 TDD corpus, which in this research question explicitly includes industrial case studies with no assigned treatment groups. The quote carries no date scope at all; pre-2011 is imported from the record's publication date, not from the text. (3) Hedge dropped and referent narrowed. few studies provided explicit details (a hedged, partial statement) becomes essentially unmeasured (a near-universal one). And a particular development process — which covers control/test-last groups as much as TDD groups — is narrowed to doing TDD. Secondary provenance point within this lens: the claim attributes the sentence to the meta-analysis, while the cited record is a Ryerson MSc thesis; the quote itself contains nothing identifying the surrounding work as a meta-analysis, so that attribution is not licensed by the quoted text either. I could not confirm the quote is verbatim page text — the figshare landing page returned HTTP 403 and the sentence would in any case live in the PDF, not the landing page, so verbatim-ness on the cited URL is unverified.

refuted.claim: The authors did not verify that participants actually followed the assigned process, and state that no empirical TDD study checks treatment conformance — meaning the treatment label 'TDD' may not correspond to what subjects did, and they flag cycle duration, duration uniformity and refactoring effort as confounds separate from test-writing order.
refuted.why: The quoted passage is faithfully transcribed, but the claim launders the authors' universal generalization — none of the empirical studies on TDD check treatment conformance — into the record as fact, and that generalization is false. It is contradicted by prior published TDD experiments, two of whose authors are co-authors of the very paper making the claim (Burak Turhan and Davide Fucci appear on arXiv 2011.11942). EXACT OVERREACH: no empirical TDD study checks treatment conformance. COUNTER-EVIDENCE (full text extracted locally to /tmp/claude-1000/-home-<user>-Desktop-Lab/9e11ce5a-30c7-475c-b67a-0bb78a03d4c7/scratchpad/conf2014.txt, from the green-OA copy at http://bura.brunel.ac.uk/bitstream/2438/14622/1/FullText.pdf): 1. Fucci, Turhan & Oivo, The Impact of Process Conformance on the Effects of Test-driven Development, ESEM 2014, DOI 10.1145/2652524.2652526. They measured conformance to the assigned TDD treatment directly: The level of conformance was calculated using the output of the Besouro tool… CONF = #episodes(TDD)/#episodes x 100. Conformance is then the percentage of the developers' episodes recognized as TDD compliant over all the episodes. They split n=22 TDD subjects at the median (85%) into high- and low-conformant groups (Section 3.5, Conformance criteria) and regressed outcomes on CONF. 2. That same paper states flatly the opposite of the Santos et al. generalization: Most of the previous studies on TDD used process conformance as a mean to check for internal validity [33, 30, 50] — i.e. Madeyski & Szala, Johnson & Kou, Wang & Erdogmus. Its related-work section adds: Madeyski and Szala [33] conducted an experiment about TDD effectiveness. In order to improve the internal validity of their study they measured process conformance, and describes Kou/Johnson's Zorro rule-based conformance classifier validated against video recordings (Zorro classified correctly 89% of the development episodes… and 85% during the second run in industrial settings), later enhanced as Besouro (Becker, Pedroso, Pimenta & Jacobi, Information and Software Technology 2015, DOI 10.1016/j.infsof.2014.06.003, Besouro: A framework for exploring compliance rules in automatic TDD behavior assessment, confirmed via Crossref). 3. Companion study: Fucci, Turhan & Oivo, Conformance factor in test-driven development, EASE 2014, DOI 10.1145/2601248.2601272 (confirmed via Crossref). MATERIAL QUALIFICATION, NOT JUST PEDANTRY: the claim's inference (meaning the treatment label 'TDD' may not correspond to what subjects did) was empirically tested by the ESEM 2014 study and did not hold — measured conformance predicted nothing: neither quality (p-value=0.21), productivity (p-value=0.80), number of tests (p-value=0.39) nor coverage (p-value = 0.09) can be regressed from the level of TDD process conformance, and none of the variables is significantly correlated with the independent variable CONF (n=22, small sample, so weak but directly on point). So the unverified-conformance worry is a real but bounded limitation, not the open field-wide hole the claim implies. The defensible version is: Santos et al. did not verify conformance in their 12 experiments, and most TDD experiments do not — but several do (Fucci/Turhan/Oivo 2014 x2; Madeyski & Szala; Kou/Johnson's Zorro; Becker et al.'s Besouro), and the one study that modeled conformance against outcomes found no relationship. METHOD NOTE: this session's WebSearch budget (200/200) and the Tavily plan quota were both exhausted before I started, so the two contradiction-seeking retrievals were run via WebFetch plus the Crossref, Semantic Scholar and arXiv APIs — searching for TDD studies that DO measure conformance (Besouro/Zorro/Fucci), and for the reference trail out of the Santos et al. citation network. Both surfaced contradiction rather than confirmation.

refuted.claim: The review reports two large in-the-wild conformance measurements showing TDD is almost never practiced strictly: Beller et al. observed 2,443 developers over 2.5 years and found only 2.2% of sessions containing test executions matched strict TDD patterns, and Borle et al. found TDD practiced in only 0.8% of 256,572 public GitHub projects that contain test files. This directly undercuts the assumption that treatment groups (or self-identified TDD adopters) actually did TDD.
refuted.why: VERBATIM CHECK PASSES: I pulled the full text (arXiv 2007.09863v1 = Ghafari, Gross, Fucci, Felderer, Why Research on Test-Driven Development is Inconclusive?, ESEM '20). The supporting quote is verbatim page text at §3.2.2 (PDF p.1, two-column line-wrapped), and every number in the claim matches exactly: 2,443 developers, 2.5 years, 2.2% of sessions with test executions, 0.8%, 256,572 GitHub projects which contain test files. The source is genuinely a secondary/review study, so the review reports is fair attribution. Two defects remain, both in the claim's framing rather than its arithmetic. (1) OVERREACH IN THE FINAL SENTENCE — the load-bearing one. The claim asserts This directly undercuts the assumption that treatment groups (or self-identified TDD adopters) actually did TDD. The quote contains zero words about controlled experiments, treatment groups, study participants, or study protocols. Both cited studies are unsupervised field observation: Beller via IDE telemetry, Borle via GitHub mining. The sentence the claim's quote CUTS OFF immediately before is the paper's own scope condition: There are a few recent studies that investigated how testing is actually done 'in the wild.' Dropping that hedge is what makes the leap possible. Lab treatment groups are trained, instructed, and monitored on the protocol — a materially different population from unsupervised developers, and the word directly claims an entailment the quote does not carry. Corroborating the gap: `grep -in conform|adhere|treatment group|control group` over the paper's full text returns no hit for conformance, treatment group, or control group anywhere; the only adherence hit (p.2, §3.2.5 area) is an unrelated list of practitioner-cited reasons. The parenthetical (or self-identified TDD adopters) IS supported by Beller's developers who claim to do TDD; the primary noun treatment groups is not. (2) MISLABELED MEASUREMENT TYPE. The claim calls these two large in-the-wild conformance measurements. Only Beller's is a conformance measurement (2.2% among sessions with test executions, from developers who claim to do TDD). Borle's 0.8% is a prevalence/base-rate figure across ALL 256,572 projects containing test files — the quote never says those projects claimed or intended to practice TDD, so it cannot bear on whether self-identified adopters conform. Relatedly, the headline gloss TDD is almost never practiced strictly universalizes Beller's doubly-restricted denominator (developers claiming TDD, sessions containing test executions). The numeric core survives intact; the claim is refuted on the unlicensed extension from field non-conformance to experimental treatment groups, and on recharacterizing a prevalence statistic as a conformance statistic.

refuted.claim: The review states, citing Fucci et al.'s dissection study, that when quality is measured the degree of iteration of the development process matters more than the test-first/test-last ordering — i.e. the measured benefit does not survive isolation of test-FIRST ordering from iteration granularity; Karac et al. corroborate by tying TDD success to sub-dividing requirements into smaller tasks (more iterations).
refuted.why: Provenance checks out; the gloss does not. I pulled the ESEM'20 PDF (arXiv 2007.09863, Why Research on Test-Driven Development is Inconclusive?, Sec. 3.2.5 Comparisons) and the supporting quote is verbatim, and the paper's own Table (p. 215 of extracted text) and bibliography entry [14] confirm the attribution to Davide Fucci, Hakan Erdogmus, Burak Turhan, Markku Oivo, Natalia Juristo, A Dissection of the Test-Driven Development Process: Does It Really Matter to Test-First or to Test-Last?, TSE 43(7), 2017 — so citing Fucci et al.'s dissection study and the paraphrase of the ranking sentence are both licensed. Two overreaches after that are not. (1) STRENGTHENING A RANKING INTO A NULL RESULT. The page says only: the degree of iteration of the process is more important than the order in which the test cases are written [14]. The claim's i.e. clause converts that into the measured benefit does not survive isolation of test-FIRST ordering from iteration granularity — i.e. that once iteration granularity is controlled, the test-first effect vanishes. More important than is a comparative weighting of two factors; it is compatible with test-first ordering retaining a real, smaller effect. The quote states no such disappearance, no controlled-isolation design, and no null finding, and the measured benefit (which benefit? on which outcome?) has no referent in the quoted text beyond the bare scope condition when measuring quality. (2) CORRELATION AND HEDGE BOTH DROPPED, PLUS A MANUFACTURED LINK. The page says Karac et al. [23] suggest that the success of TDD is correlated with the sub-division of a requirement into smaller tasks. The claim renders this as Karac et al. corroborate by tying TDD success to sub-dividing requirements — dropping the author's hedge (suggest), dropping correlated, and promoting a suggested correlation into corroborating evidence for the (already overstated) null-effect claim in clause one. The source presents the Fucci sentence and the Karac sentence as two adjacent observations in a factor inventory; it never says Karac corroborates Fucci, and Karac et al. [23] is a task-description-granularity experiment, not a replication or isolation of Fucci's test-first/test-last contrast. Clause one alone would pass. As stated, the claim asserts a null-effect-under-isolation result and a corroboration relationship that the quoted page text does not contain.

refuted.claim: The review reports that Munir et al.'s systematic review used rigor and relevance as an explicit stratifier and found that the subset of studies scoring high on both rigor and relevance shows improvement in external quality but at the cost of degraded productivity — making study rigor/relevance an empirically applied moderator rather than a merely asserted one.
refuted.why: The supporting quote IS verbatim in the source (confirmed by extracting arXiv:2007.09863's PDF: the sentence appears in Ghafari et al.'s related-work paragraph, not in their five factor categories). Provenance is clean. The claim fails on substance in two ways, both established by credible independent sources. OVERREACH 1 — the high rigor AND relevance quadrant is made of NON-EXPERIMENTAL studies, and every quadrant containing controlled experiments shows the opposite. Santos, Vegas, Uyaguari, Dieste, Turhan & Juristo (2020), Software Quality Journal 28:371-395, doi:10.1007/s11219-020-09512-3, §2.2, describe Munir et al.'s actual 2x2 grid in detail: The nine studies in the high rigor and relevance category (industry and academic case studies and surveys) show improvements in external quality. Studies with high relevance and low rigor (industry and academic case studies) obtained similar results. Studies with low relevance and high rigor (experiments and one case study with students) mostly show no differences in terms of external quality between TDD and other development approaches. So Munir's high rigor + high relevance cell is nine case studies and surveys — no random assignment, self-selected adopters — while the cell holding the controlled experiments shows NO difference in external quality. Because Ivarsson & Gorschek's relevance score rewards industrial setting and realism, it structurally demotes controlled experiments to low relevance. The stratifier is therefore confounded with study design, not a clean quality moderator. The claim's load-bearing gloss — an empirically applied moderator rather than a merely asserted one — invites the reader to conclude that the methodologically strongest evidence supports TDD's quality benefit, when in Munir's own grid the reverse holds: the experiments show no difference. Santos et al. say so explicitly at §2.2: The above reviews include different types of empirical studies on TDD (surveys, case studies, experiments, etc.). This might have had an impact on the conclusions reached. Also note Santos et al., surveying all four quadrants, attach no productivity result to that cell at all. OVERREACH 2 — an independent rigor stratification of the same literature reverses the sign on BOTH outcomes. Tosun, Ahmed, Turhan & Juristo (2018), On the effectiveness of unit tests in test-driven development, ICSSP '18, doi:10.1145/3202710.3203153, §1, summarizing Turhan et al.'s review: When studies of high rigor, i.e., controlled experiments and pilot studies designed with good constructs in medium to large scale studies, were considered, the results on quality remains inconsistent, whereas the results on productivity seems to be improving with TDD. That is the exact opposite of Munir's high-rigor/high-relevance cell (quality improved, productivity degraded) on both variables. The same page also reports Rafique & Misic's meta-analysis (IEEE TSE 39(6)) finding TDD has a positive effect on external quality, but little or no effect on productivity — contradicting the degrading productivity half specifically. Two secondary studies stratifying overlapping primary literature by rigor reach opposing conclusions, so rigor/relevance is a contested and unreplicated stratifier, not a settled empirically applied moderator. Net: the claim may be used as Ghafari et al. report X about Munir, but not as rigor/relevance is an empirically validated moderator showing quality up / productivity down.
